new_statements.quote: In Nakkara, stress is not contrastive, and therefore not phonemic. ... In simple word-forms, the domain of stress in Nakkara is not the word as such but the morpheme, usually the root morpheme. ... Verbal and nominal prefixes and suffixes, although morphemes in their own right are not assigned primary stress. ... it is normal for primary stress to be assigned to the first syllable of the root morpheme, and accompanying primary stress is noticeable lengthening of the vowel. This generalisation of primary stress assignment applies to over 95% of the data. Secondary stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable and then on alternating syllables preceding the penultimate (i.e. in a right-to-left direction)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Non-contrastive, predictable stress: primary stress falls on the first syllable of the root morpheme (prefixes and suffixes do not take primary stress), accompanied by vowel lengthening; in unprefixed monomorphemic words this is the word-initial syllable. Formalised (2.5.1) as a left-headed binary foot over the first two root syllables, then feet from the margins inward, a left-headed unbounded tree over the stem and a right-headed one over the prefix string; word-initial syllabic consonants are extrametrical.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the penultimate syllable and on alternating syllables leftward from it, but never on the syllable immediately after the primary-stressed syllable; prefix strings also receive secondary (foot-level) prominence on their first two syllables per Stress Rule 1(b).
new_statements.exceptions: Rule covers >95% of data; monosyllabic verb complexes are 'somewhat of an exception' (see 6.2); a small set of words has irregular primary stress, marked with an acute accent in the orthography; in two-root compound nominals primary stress is on the first root in ~73% of cases, otherwise on the second root; in compounds with three or more roots primary stress is usually on the second root.
new_statements.domain_note: Author states the domain of stress is the (root) morpheme rather than the word; statements are about word-level stress in elicited word-forms (up to 13 syllables); stress is not marked in the practical orthography except irregular cases. Contrasted with Ndjebbana where stress is said to be less regular and partly contrastive (p. 1.1 and end of 2.5).
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Nakkara (= Glottolog Nakara, naka1260) as spoken around Maningrida; no dialect split is made. Eather contrasts Nakkara's regular stress with neighbouring Ndjebbana (djee1236), where stress is said to be less regular and partly contrastive.
